title: Kidney, Urinary Tract & Endocrine
summary: Learn the filtering architecture of the kidney, the urinary tract and the hormone-making glands.

lessons.title: Glomerulus & the Filtration Barrier

levels.kid:
Your two kidneys clean your blood all day long. Inside each kidney are about a million tiny filters. Each filter starts with a little ball of very thin blood tubes called a **glomerulus** (say it: glow-MARE-you-lus).

The ball sits inside a cup, like a fist pushed into a soft balloon. Blood squeezes through the walls of the tiny tubes. Water, salt and sugar slip through into the cup. Big things, like blood cells and proteins, are too big to fit, so they stay in the blood.

The filter has three layers, like three sieves stacked together. The last layer is made of cells with little "feet" that hold hands and leave tiny slits between them.
levels.hs:
The working unit of the kidney is the **nephron**, and each human kidney has roughly a million of them. A nephron begins with a **renal corpuscle**, which has two parts:
- The **glomerulus**: a tuft of looping capillaries fed by an **afferent arteriole** and drained by an **efferent arteriole**.
- **Bowman's capsule**: a double-walled cup around the tuft. The space between its walls, **Bowman's space**, collects the filtered fluid, called **filtrate**.

Blood pressure pushes plasma out of the capillaries. Before it reaches Bowman's space, it must cross the **filtration barrier**, which has three layers:
- **Fenestrated endothelium**: capillary cells full of small holes (fenestrae).
- **Glomerular basement membrane (GBM)**: a thick shared sheet of matrix.
- **Podocytes**: cells of the inner capsule wall that wrap the capillaries with interlocking **foot processes**. The narrow gaps between them are **filtration slits**, bridged by a thin **slit diaphragm**.

Water, glucose, ions and urea pass through easily. Blood cells and large proteins like **albumin** mostly stay behind. A real example: in **nephrotic syndrome**, podocyte foot processes flatten and the barrier leaks protein, so large amounts of protein appear in the urine and the body swells. Healthy kidneys filter about 180 liters of plasma a day.
levels.college:
Under the light microscope, the renal corpuscle appears in the cortex as a rounded cluster of capillary loops surrounded by a clear crescent, Bowman's space, and a thin outer rim of simple squamous **parietal epithelium**. The corpuscle has a **vascular pole**, where the arterioles enter and leave, and a **urinary pole**, where Bowman's space opens into the proximal tubule.

**Cell types in the tuft:**
- **Endothelial cells**: fenestrae of about 70-100 nm with no diaphragms. They are coated by a negatively charged **glycocalyx**.
- **Podocytes**: the **visceral epithelium**. Large cell bodies bulge into Bowman's space. Primary processes branch into interdigitating foot processes.
- **Mesangial cells**: modified smooth-muscle-like cells in the stalk between capillaries. They make matrix, phagocytose trapped proteins, and contract to adjust filtration surface area.

**The barrier, layer by layer:**
- The GBM is about 300-350 nm thick in adults. It forms from fused endothelial and podocyte basal laminae, and on electron microscopy shows a lamina rara interna, a lamina densa and a lamina rara externa. Its main components are **type IV collagen** (α3α4α5 network), laminin-521, nidogen and heparan sulfate proteoglycans.
- The slit diaphragm spans gaps of about 30-40 nm. It is built mainly from **nephrin** and **NEPH1**, anchored by **podocin** and CD2AP to the actin cytoskeleton.

**Selectivity** depends on size, shape and charge. Molecules under about 2 nm in radius filter freely. Above roughly 4 nm, filtration is negligible. Albumin, at about 3.6 nm radius and negatively charged, is largely retained.

**Forces:** filtration follows Starling forces. Glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure (about 55 mmHg) is opposed by Bowman's space pressure and plasma oncotic pressure, giving a net pressure of roughly 10 mmHg. Because there are arterioles at both ends, the tuft is held at an unusually high pressure.

Special stains help on slides. PAS and silver (Jones) stains outline the GBM, which reveals thickening or "spikes."
levels.phd:
How the glomerular barrier achieves its permselectivity is still debated. The classic charge-selectivity model came from Brenner and Deen's 1970s dextran sieving studies. Anionic dextrans were filtered less than neutral ones of the same size, which was attributed to fixed negative charges from heparan sulfate (perlecan, agrin) and podocalyxin. This model has been challenged. Dextrans adopt flexible, elongated shapes and are taken up by cells, which confounds the measurements. Mice lacking GBM heparan sulfate do not develop major proteinuria. Most investigators now treat charge as a modest contributor, with size and shape dominant.

All three layers act in series, but where the main sieve lies is contested:
- **Slit-diaphragm primacy.** Rodewald and Karnovsky (1974) described a zipper-like structure with roughly 4 × 14 nm pores. Mutations in **NPHS1** (nephrin) cause congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type, and **NPHS2** (podocin) mutations cause steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome. Both point to the slit diaphragm.
- **GBM as a gel.** Smithies proposed a gel permeation/diffusion model, in which albumin concentration is polarized at the GBM. Miner's group showed that mice lacking **laminin β2** (Pierson syndrome in humans) leak protein before podocyte effacement appears.
- **Electrokinetic hypothesis.** Moeller and colleagues proposed that filtration generates streaming potentials across the barrier that oppose anion passage.

How much albumin is filtered also remains uncertain. Intravital two-photon studies by Russo and colleagues (2007) suggested glomerular sieving coefficients near 0.03. Micropuncture and later intravital work give values around 0.0006. The difference matters, because the high value implies massive proximal tubular retrieval by **megalin-cubilin** receptors.

Podocytes are terminally differentiated and replace themselves poorly. Their structure depends on signaling through **synaptopodin**, α-actinin-4 (ACTN4), TRPC6 calcium channels and Rho GTPases. Podocytes and endothelium also talk to each other. Podocyte-derived **VEGF-A** maintains endothelial fenestrae, which explains the glomerular thrombotic microangiopathy and proteinuria seen with anti-VEGF cancer drugs. Losing podocytes beyond roughly 20-40% drives glomerulosclerosis, as Wiggins described in podocyte-depletion models.
levels.expert:
In renal pathology, the glomerulus is read with three tools together: light microscopy (H&E, PAS, Jones silver, trichrome), immunofluorescence and electron microscopy. Each layer of the barrier has its own signature diseases:
- **Podocytopathies.** In minimal change disease, light microscopy looks normal. The only lesion is diffuse foot-process effacement on EM. Anti-nephrin autoantibodies, reported in 2022 by Watts and colleagues, now link part of this disease to autoimmunity. FSGS shows segmental sclerosis. It is classified as primary (circulating factor), genetic, maladaptive (hyperfiltration) or secondary (APOL1 variants, viruses), and the category guides treatment and the risk of recurrence after transplant.
- **GBM diseases.** Alport syndrome comes from COL4A3/4/5 mutations and shows a split, basket-weave lamina densa. Thin basement membrane nephropathy shows a GBM under about 250 nm. In anti-GBM disease, autoantibodies target the α3 NC1 domain, giving linear IgG staining on immunofluorescence. In **membranous nephropathy**, subepithelial deposits cause silver-stain "spikes." Beck and Salant's 2009 discovery of **PLA2R** antibodies made a serologic diagnosis possible, and THSD7A and NELL1 have since been added as antigens.
- **Endothelial injury.** Thrombotic microangiopathy shows endotheliosis and double contours of the GBM. Preeclampsia, linked to excess sFlt-1 that blocks VEGF, is a classic cause.

Common pitfalls:
- Tangential sections make the GBM look falsely thick.
- Effacement is a nonspecific response, not a diagnosis.
- An inadequate biopsy (fewer than about 10 glomeruli) can miss segmental FSGS.

On the research side, glomerulus-on-chip devices and kidney organoids now form podocyte-like cells with slit diaphragms, though their GBM maturation is incomplete. Cryo-electron tomography of the slit diaphragm, published in 2021-2023, revealed a fishnet-like nephrin and NEPH1 meshwork. Treatments aimed at the podocyte are entering trials: TRPC6 and TRPC5 inhibitors, APOL1 inhibitors such as inaxaplin, and anti-CD20 therapy for antibody-mediated podocytopathies. SGLT2 inhibitors protect the glomerulus by restoring tubuloglomerular feedback and reducing hyperfiltration. A key open question is whether adult parietal epithelial progenitors can really regenerate podocytes, or whether lost podocytes are mostly permanent.

keyPoints: The renal corpuscle is the glomerular capillary tuft plus Bowman's capsule
Afferent and efferent arterioles keep glomerular pressure high
The barrier is fenestrated endothelium, the GBM and podocyte slit diaphragms
Nephrin and podocin build the slit diaphragm; mutations cause nephrotic syndrome
Size and shape matter most for selectivity; albumin is largely retained
Mesangial cells support the tuft, clear debris and adjust surface area

test.q: Which vessel carries blood into the glomerular tuft?
test.explain: The afferent arteriole delivers blood to the tuft. The efferent arteriole drains it, which keeps pressure in the tuft high.

test.q: Which cells form the visceral layer of Bowman's capsule?
test.explain: Podocytes wrap the capillaries with foot processes. The parietal layer is the outer simple squamous wall.

test.q: What is the correct order of barrier layers from blood to Bowman's space?
test.explain: Filtrate crosses the fenestrated endothelium, then the basement membrane, then the podocyte slit diaphragms.

test.q: Which protein is a key structural part of the slit diaphragm?
test.explain: Nephrin, together with NEPH1 and podocin, builds the slit diaphragm. NPHS1 mutations cause Finnish-type congenital nephrotic syndrome.

test.q: Which collagen type is the main structural component of the GBM?
test.explain: Type IV collagen (the α3α4α5 network) forms the GBM scaffold. Types I-III are fibrillar collagens found elsewhere.

test.q: In nephrotic syndrome, what happens to the podocyte foot processes?
test.explain: Foot-process effacement makes the barrier leak, so large amounts of protein appear in the urine.

test.q: What is one function of mesangial cells?
choices: Clearing trapped proteins from the tuft
test.explain: Mesangial cells phagocytose trapped proteins, make matrix and contract to adjust filtration area.

test.q: Which molecule is largely held back by a healthy barrier?
test.explain: Albumin (radius about 3.6 nm, negatively charged) is mostly retained. Small solutes like glucose, urea and sodium filter freely.

test.q: Which stain outlines the GBM well on a slide?
test.explain: PAS and Jones silver stains highlight basement membranes. Congo red is used for amyloid.

test.q: The fluid collected in Bowman's space is called ___.
test.explain: Plasma that crosses the barrier becomes filtrate, which then flows into the proximal tubule.

test.q: What is the name for the functional unit of the kidney, about a million per kidney?
test.explain: Each nephron begins with a renal corpuscle and continues as the tubule.

test.q: Glomerular endothelial cells are ___, meaning they are full of small pores.
test.explain: Fenestrae of about 70-100 nm let plasma pass freely while blood cells stay behind.

kidTest.q: What does the kidney's tiny filter do?
kidTest.explain: The filters clean your blood.

kidTest.q: What sits inside the cup of the filter?
choices: A ball of tiny blood tubes
A small pocket of trapped air
A tiny chip of soft bone
kidTest.explain: The glomerulus is a ball of tiny blood tubes inside the cup.

kidTest.q: Which of these is too big to get through the filter?
kidTest.explain: Red blood cells are too big to get through the filter, so they stay in the blood. Salt and water are small enough to pass through.

kidTest.q: How many layers does the filter have?
kidTest.explain: There are three layers, like three stacked sieves.

kidTest.q: The filter cells have little ___ that hold hands. Hint: f _ _ t
kidTest.explain: Podocytes have foot processes with tiny slits between them.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking GBM heparan sulfate show little proteinuria. What does this most weaken?
choices: The role of nephrin at the slit diaphragm
The Starling model of filtration forces
The role of megalin in tubular uptake
The view that charge dominates selectivity
advancedTest.explain: If removing fixed anionic charge barely causes leak, charge cannot be the main determinant of selectivity. Size and shape matter more.

advancedTest.q: A patient on anti-VEGF therapy develops proteinuria with endothelial injury. What is the best explanation?
choices: Direct toxicity that destroys type IV collagen
Loss of podocyte VEGF support for the endothelium
Megalin blockade in the proximal tubule
Mesangial cells contracting and closing slits
advancedTest.explain: Podocyte-derived VEGF-A maintains endothelial fenestrae. Blocking it causes thrombotic microangiopathy and proteinuria.

advancedTest.q: If the glomerular albumin sieving coefficient were truly about 0.03, what would follow?
choices: The tubules would need to retrieve huge amounts
The slit diaphragm would play little role
The GBM would be thicker than normal
advancedTest.explain: A high sieving coefficient means a lot of albumin is filtered. To keep urine nearly protein-free, megalin-cubilin uptake in the proximal tubule would have to be very large.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows normal light microscopy but diffuse effacement on EM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
advancedTest.explain: Minimal change disease shows effacement alone. Membranous shows silver-stain spikes, Alport a split GBM, and anti-GBM disease linear IgG.

lessons.title: Tubules, Collecting Ducts & the Juxtaglomerular Apparatus

levels.kid:
Your kidney makes a watery liquid from your blood. Then that liquid flows through millions of tiny tubes, like long twisty straws. As it flows, the tubes take back the good stuff your body needs, like sugar, salt and water. What is left over becomes pee.

Each part of the tube has its own job. The first part is a hard worker with fuzzy brushes on its cells to grab lots of good stuff. Later parts fine-tune how much salt and water you keep.

There is also a tiny checkpoint where the tube touches the little blood ball that filters the blood. It is like a guard who tastes the salt in the liquid. If something is off, it sends a signal to fix your blood pressure.
levels.hs:
After blood is filtered in the glomerulus, the filtrate enters the **renal tubule**, a long tube where most of it is reabsorbed back into the blood. Under the microscope, each segment looks different because its cells do different jobs.

- **Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)**: cuboidal cells with a fuzzy **brush border** of microvilli and pink cytoplasm packed with mitochondria. It reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered salt and water, and nearly all the glucose and amino acids.
- **Loop of Henle**: dips toward the center of the kidney. Its thin limbs are lined by flat **simple squamous** cells; the thick ascending limb pumps out salt and makes the surrounding tissue salty.
- **Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)**: cuboidal cells with no brush border, so its lumen looks clean and wide.
- **Collecting duct**: pale cells with sharp borders between them. Here the hormone **ADH** (antidiuretic hormone) decides how much water you keep.

Where the distal tubule touches its own glomerulus sits the **juxtaglomerular apparatus (JGA)**. The **macula densa** senses salt in the tubule, and **juxtaglomerular (granular) cells** in the arteriole wall release **renin**, the enzyme that starts a chain raising blood pressure.

Example: when you are dehydrated, ADH makes collecting ducts insert water channels, so your urine becomes darker and more concentrated.
levels.college:
The nephron's tubular segments are recognizable by epithelial height, apical specializations and basal features, all reflecting transport function.

**Proximal tubule.** Tall cuboidal, intensely eosinophilic cells with a PAS-positive **brush border**, apical endocytic vesicles, and basal **plasma membrane infoldings** interdigitating with elongated mitochondria (basal striations). Lateral borders are indistinct because the cells interdigitate. The lumen often looks ragged. It reabsorbs ~65% of filtered Na+ and water via Na+/K+-ATPase–driven secondary transport (SGLT2 for glucose, NHE3 for Na+/H+), plus megalin/cubilin-mediated protein uptake.

**Loop of Henle.** Thin limbs: simple squamous, resembling capillaries but without red cells. The descending thin limb is water-permeable (aquaporin-1). The **thick ascending limb** is cuboidal, water-impermeable, and uses **NKCC2** to drive the countercurrent multiplier that builds medullary hypertonicity.

**Distal convoluted tubule.** Lower cuboidal, less eosinophilic cells, no brush border, more nuclei per cross-section, clear lumen. Reabsorbs Na+ and Cl- through **NCC**, the target of thiazides.

**Collecting duct.** Cuboidal to columnar cells with crisp lateral borders and pale cytoplasm.
- **Principal cells**: ENaC sodium channels (regulated by aldosterone) and **aquaporin-2** (inserted under ADH via V2 receptors).
- **Intercalated cells**: darker, mitochondria-rich; type A secrete H+, type B secrete HCO3-.

**Juxtaglomerular apparatus** at the vascular pole:
- **Macula densa**: crowded, tall cells in the DCT wall (start of distal tubule) that sense luminal NaCl via NKCC2.
- **Juxtaglomerular cells**: modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole containing renin granules.
- **Extraglomerular mesangial (lacis) cells** between them.
Low NaCl delivery or low perfusion pressure triggers renin release, activating the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS).
levels.phd:
Segmental tubular morphology is a direct readout of transport physiology. Proximal tubule cells are rich in mitochondria (though the DCT and thick ascending limb are even denser) because Na+/K+-ATPase consumes most renal O2; this makes the **S3 segment** (pars recta, outer stripe of outer medulla) exceptionally vulnerable to ischemia, where relatively high metabolic demand coincides with a marginal O2 supply. The proximal tubule is subdivided into S1-S3: S1 has the tallest brush border and most elaborate endocytic apparatus, while S3 has a long brush border but fewer basolateral infoldings. Megalin and cubilin form the endocytic receptor complex retrieving filtered albumin, vitamin-binding proteins and light chains, which is why proximal cells load with protein droplets in proteinuria.

The thick ascending limb secretes **uromodulin** (Tamm-Horsfall protein), the most abundant urinary protein and the matrix of hyaline casts. Its paracellular pathway, governed by claudin-16 and claudin-19, carries Mg2+ and Ca2+ driven by a lumen-positive voltage from K+ recycling through ROMK; mutations cause familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria.

The **connecting tubule** and cortical collecting duct carry the aldosterone-sensitive distal nephron: mineralocorticoid receptor specificity is protected by 11β-HSD2, which inactivates cortisol. ENaC upregulation underlies Liddle syndrome. ADH acting on V2 receptors raises cAMP, PKA phosphorylates AQP2 at Ser256, and vesicles fuse apically; AQP3/4 provide basolateral exit. Inner medullary collecting ducts also express UT-A1 urea transporters, recycling urea to sustain medullary osmolality.

JGA signaling links two feedback loops. **Tubuloglomerular feedback** (TGF): increased NaCl at the macula densa enters via NKCC2, ATP is released basolaterally, converted to adenosine, which acts on A1 receptors to constrict the afferent arteriole and lower single-nephron GFR. Low NaCl instead stimulates COX-2 and nNOS in macula densa cells, promoting renin release through PGE2 and EP receptors. Renin secretion from granular cells is also triggered by an intrarenal baroreceptor and by β1-adrenergic sympathetic input, and is unusual in being stimulated by cAMP but inhibited by intracellular Ca2+, the reverse of most secretory cells. Renin-lineage tracing studies by Sequeira-López and Gomez showed that renin cells can recruit along arterioles under homeostatic stress.
levels.expert:
Clinically, tubule histology is read most often on renal biopsy. **Acute tubular injury** shows loss of brush border, epithelial flattening, luminal sloughed cells and granular casts; findings are frequently subtle and correlate poorly with serum creatinine, and autolysis can mimic brush border loss. Distinguishing features: **isometric vacuolization** in proximal cells suggests osmotic injury (classically from mannitol, sucrose-containing IVIG or contrast media) or calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity. **Myeloma cast nephropathy** produces fractured, PAS-weak casts in distal segments with giant-cell reaction, as light chains coprecipitate with uromodulin. Tubulitis, with lymphocytes crossing the tubular basement membrane, is graded in Banff classification for transplant rejection and is also seen in acute interstitial nephritis, often drug-induced (e.g., proton-pump inhibitors, β-lactams).

For a pharmacology mind, the nephron is a map of diuretic targets: acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase, PCT), loop diuretics (NKCC2, TAL), thiazides (NCC, DCT), amiloride and triamterene (ENaC), spironolactone and finerenone (mineralocorticoid receptor), and tolvaptan (V2 antagonist, used in hyponatremia and autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, where cysts largely derive from collecting ducts). SGLT2 inhibitors act on the S1-S2 proximal tubule; their kidney protection is attributed partly to restored TGF, because higher NaCl delivery to the macula densa constricts the afferent arteriole and reduces glomerular hyperfiltration. Lithium enters principal cells via ENaC and causes nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, explaining amiloride's protective use.

Recent advances: single-cell and spatial transcriptomics (KPMP, HuBMAP atlases) defined injured proximal tubule states, notably **failed-repair** cells expressing VCAM1, which persist after acute injury and drive fibrosis and progression to chronic kidney disease. Intercalated cells are now known to function in innate defense and possibly interconvert with principal cells. Open questions include how far the JGA renin-cell reserve contributes to chronic RAAS blockade response, whether renin cells become pathogenic arteriolar myofibroblasts, and whether tubular injury biomarkers such as KIM-1 and NGAL improve decisions beyond histology.

Pitfall: in neurosurgical patients, hyponatremia from SIADH versus cerebral salt wasting hinges on collecting duct ADH action versus natriuresis; volume status, not urine sodium alone, separates them.

keyPoints: The proximal tubule has a brush border and reabsorbs about two-thirds of filtered salt and water
Thin limbs are simple squamous; the thick ascending limb (NKCC2) builds medullary salt
The distal tubule lacks a brush border; NCC is the thiazide target
Collecting ducts have principal cells (ENaC, aquaporin-2 under ADH) and intercalated cells (acid-base)
The JGA = macula densa, renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells and extraglomerular mesangial cells
Macula densa NaCl sensing drives tubuloglomerular feedback and renin release

test.q: Which feature best identifies the proximal convoluted tubule on a slide?
choices: Crowded tall nuclei at one spot
test.explain: The PCT's microvilli form a brush border that increases surface area for reabsorption. Pale cells with crisp borders describe the collecting duct.

test.q: About how much of the filtered sodium and water is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule?
test.explain: The proximal tubule reabsorbs roughly 65% of filtered Na+ and water.

test.q: The thin limbs of the loop of Henle are lined by which epithelium?
test.explain: Thin limbs are simple squamous and can resemble capillaries, but contain no red blood cells.

test.q: Which transporter of the thick ascending limb is blocked by loop diuretics?
test.explain: NKCC2 drives salt reabsorption in the thick ascending limb. NCC is the thiazide target in the distal tubule.

test.q: Under ADH, collecting duct principal cells insert which water channel into their apical membrane?
test.explain: ADH acting via V2 receptors moves aquaporin-2 vesicles into the apical membrane; aquaporin-3 and -4 sit basolaterally.

test.q: Which cells in the collecting duct handle acid-base balance?
test.explain: Intercalated cells secrete H+ (type A) or bicarbonate (type B). Principal cells mainly handle Na+ and water.

test.q: The macula densa is a specialized region of which segment?
test.explain: The macula densa lies where the distal tubule contacts its own glomerulus's vascular pole.

test.q: Where are renin-secreting juxtaglomerular cells located?
test.explain: JG (granular) cells are modified smooth muscle cells of the afferent arteriole that store renin.

test.q: How does the distal convoluted tubule look compared with the proximal tubule?
choices: Paler cells with a clear lumen
Layered cells with a thick crust
test.explain: The DCT has lower, less eosinophilic cells without a brush border, so its lumen looks clean and wide.

test.q: Juxtaglomerular cells release the enzyme ___, which starts the RAAS cascade.
test.explain: Renin release begins the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system that raises blood pressure.

test.q: Which hormone (abbreviation) increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct?
test.explain: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) inserts aquaporin-2 water channels.

test.q: Aldosterone increases sodium entry through ___ channels in principal cells.
test.explain: ENaC, the epithelial sodium channel, is upregulated by aldosterone.

kidTest.q: What do the kidney's tiny tubes do with good stuff like sugar?
choices: Take it back into the body
kidTest.explain: The tubes take back what your body needs.

kidTest.q: What does the first part of the tube have on its cells?
kidTest.explain: Fuzzy brushes help it grab lots of good stuff.

kidTest.q: What is left in the tubes at the end?
kidTest.explain: The leftover liquid becomes pee.

kidTest.q: What does the tiny checkpoint 'taste'?
kidTest.explain: It senses salt and helps fix blood pressure.

kidTest.q: The kidney's long thin pipes are called t _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: The liquid flows through tiny tubes.

advancedTest.q: Why is the S3 proximal tubule segment especially vulnerable in ischemic injury?
choices: High O2 demand meets marginal O2 delivery
It has no basement membrane to anchor its cells
It is directly exposed to concentrated urea
It lacks mitochondria and relies on glycolysis
advancedTest.explain: S3 in the outer medulla has high transport demand yet relatively poor O2 delivery. It does not lack mitochondria.

advancedTest.q: SGLT2 inhibitors raise NaCl delivery to the macula densa. What renal effect follows?
choices: Increased renin release from granular cells
Suppressed ADH and loss of aquaporin-2
Efferent dilation that raises glomerular pressure
advancedTest.explain: Restored tubuloglomerular feedback via adenosine and A1 receptors constricts the afferent arteriole, reducing hyperfiltration.

advancedTest.q: Amiloride helps in lithium-induced nephrogenic diabetes insipidus mainly because it:
choices: Activates V2 receptors to restore aquaporin-2 insertion
Blocks ENaC, limiting lithium entry into principal cells
Inhibits NKCC2 so the medulla regains its osmolality
Increases renin to boost aldosterone action
advancedTest.explain: Lithium enters principal cells through ENaC; blocking ENaC reduces its intracellular accumulation.

advancedTest.q: Renin granular cells differ from most secretory cells in that secretion is:
choices: Promoted by cAMP but inhibited by intracellular Ca2+
Driven mostly by luminal glucose levels
Triggered by high NaCl at the macula densa
advancedTest.explain: Granular cells show the calcium paradox: Ca2+ inhibits renin release, while cAMP (e.g., via β1 or PGE2) stimulates it. High NaCl suppresses rather than triggers renin.

lessons.title: Ureter, Bladder & Urothelium

levels.kid:
After your kidneys clean your blood, they make pee. The pee has to travel down two thin tubes called **ureters** into a stretchy bag called the **bladder**. Then it leaves through one more tube, the **urethra**.

The bladder has a very special lining. It is like a raincoat that can stretch. When the bladder is empty, the lining cells are plump and round, like marshmallows stacked up. When it fills, the cells flatten out, like dough rolled thin.

The top cells are called **umbrella cells**. They keep pee from leaking back into your body, just like an umbrella keeps rain off you.

Under the lining are muscles that squeeze. They push pee along the ureters in waves, like squeezing toothpaste.
levels.hs:
Urine made in the kidney flows from the **renal pelvis** down the **ureters** to the **urinary bladder**, then out through the **urethra**. Under the microscope, these organs share a special lining called **urothelium** (also called transitional epithelium).

Urothelium is a **stratified epithelium**, meaning it has several layers of cells. It has an unusual trick: it changes shape.
- In an **empty bladder**, it looks about 5-7 cells thick, and the top cells are large and dome-shaped.
- In a **full bladder**, the cells stretch and flatten, so the lining looks only 2-3 cells thick.

The top layer is made of **umbrella cells**. They are huge, sometimes with two nuclei, and their surface membrane is stiffened by proteins called **uroplakins**. This makes the lining nearly waterproof, so the salty, acidic urine cannot seep back into tissues.

Beneath the urothelium is connective tissue (the **lamina propria**) and then smooth muscle. The bladder's thick, criss-crossing muscle is called the **detrusor muscle**. It contracts to empty the bladder.

The ureter moves urine by **peristalsis**, waves of muscle contraction, not just by gravity. That is why urine still reaches the bladder when you lie down. A kidney stone stuck in the ureter triggers strong contractions against the blockage, which is one reason the pain can be so intense.
levels.college:
The urinary passages (calyces, renal pelvis, ureters, bladder and proximal urethra) share a common three-layer plan: **mucosa** (urothelium plus lamina propria), **muscularis** and **adventitia** or serosa.

**Urothelium.** It has three cell populations:
- **Basal cells**: small, resting on the basement membrane; the stem/progenitor pool.
- **Intermediate cells**: several layers, polygonal.
- **Umbrella (superficial) cells**: very large, often binucleate or polyploid, each covering several intermediate cells.

The apical surface of umbrella cells is covered by **asymmetric unit membrane (AUM)**, rigid plaques of **uroplakin** proteins (UPIa, UPIb, UPII, UPIIIa). Seen by TEM, these plaques alternate with flexible **hinge regions**, giving a scalloped surface. Combined with tight junctions and a glycosaminoglycan surface layer, AUM creates one of the body's tightest permeability barriers to water, urea and protons.

**Accommodating stretch.** On filling, umbrella cells flatten and **fusiform vesicles** carrying uroplakin plaques fuse with the apical membrane, adding surface area. On voiding, the extra membrane is retrieved by endocytosis.

**Ureter.** It has a star-shaped lumen in cross-section, from mucosal folds. Its muscularis is classically described as **inner longitudinal and outer circular**, the reverse of the gut; the distal third adds an outer longitudinal layer. Peristalsis begins at pacemaker cells in the renal pelvis.

**Bladder.** The detrusor has three poorly separated smooth muscle layers. The **trigone**, between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice, has a smooth mucosa that stays smooth when the bladder is empty. The ureters enter **obliquely** through the bladder wall, forming a flap valve that limits reflux.

**Urethra.** It shifts from urothelium to stratified or pseudostratified columnar epithelium, then to stratified squamous epithelium near the external opening.
levels.phd:
The urothelial barrier depends on several features working together. **Uroplakins** are tetraspanins (UPIa, UPIb) that pair with single-pass partners (UPII, UPIIIa or IIIb). These heterodimers form 16-nm particles, and the particles pack in hexagonal arrays into **urothelial plaques** about 0.3-0.5 µm across. Cryo-EM work by Sun, Kong and colleagues showed that these plaques make the outer leaflet unusually thick and rigid. Tight junctions rich in claudin-4, -8 and -12 seal the gaps between cells, and the apical membrane is rich in cholesterol and cerebrosides. As a result, transepithelial resistance often exceeds 20,000-75,000 Ω·cm², among the highest of any epithelium.

Knockout mice show that uroplakins matter. Mice lacking UPIIIa or UPII lose their plaques and develop leaky urothelium, **vesicoureteral reflux** and hydronephrosis. UPIa is also the receptor used by the **FimH adhesin** on type 1 pili of uropathogenic *E. coli*. After binding, bacteria are internalized and form **intracellular bacterial communities**. In response, the urothelium sheds infected umbrella cells. Bacteria that survive the shedding can persist in underlying cells as quiescent reservoirs. This model helps explain why bladder infections often come back.

The urothelium is more than a barrier; it also senses. Umbrella cells release **ATP** when stretched, acting on P2X3 receptors on suburothelial afferents. They also express TRP channels and **PIEZO1**, and release acetylcholine and nitric oxide. Together these signals shape the micturition reflex. Suburothelial interstitial cells (PDGFRα+) may help relay these signals.

In the ureter, peristalsis begins at **atypical smooth muscle cells** in the renal pelvis. These pacemakers use **HCN channels** (I_h). Interstitial cells of the kind marked by c-Kit may also contribute.

Urothelial renewal is normally very slow, with turnover on the order of months to a year. When injured, the urothelium regenerates quickly. Lineage-tracing studies disagree on which cells drive repair. Some point to **Krt5+ basal cells**, while others show that intermediate cells, marked by **Shh** and Upk-lineage markers, regenerate the umbrella layer. Shh-to-Wnt signaling between epithelium and stroma drives this proliferation.
levels.expert:
Histopathology of the urinary tract depends on recognizing normal urothelium and its mimics.

**Diagnostic morphology.** Normal urothelium keeps its **polarity**: nuclei are oriented perpendicular to the basement membrane, and the umbrella layer matures in order toward the lumen. In **urothelial carcinoma in situ (CIS)**, nuclei are enlarged and pleomorphic, and the cells are poorly cohesive, so they shed and leave a "denuding cystitis" appearance. The umbrella layer may persist over CIS, so its presence does not exclude malignancy. A useful immunohistochemical panel is **CK20** (normally confined to umbrella cells but full-thickness in CIS), **p53** (aberrant staining) and **CD44** (normally basal, lost in CIS). Most urothelial carcinomas are **GATA3**-positive, and many express uroplakin II, which helps identify metastases of unknown primary origin.

**Benign variants.** Several patterns can mislead a pathologist:
- **Von Brunn nests** are islands of urothelium that have budded down into the lamina propria.
- **Cystitis cystica and glandularis** form when these nests develop cyst-like spaces or glandular cells.
- **Squamous metaplasia** of the trigone is common in women and is usually physiological.
- **Nephrogenic adenoma** comes from implanted renal tubular cells (PAX8+) and can mimic adenocarcinoma.

**Staging relies on wall anatomy.** The muscularis mucosae in the bladder is thin and discontinuous. In biopsies, its smooth muscle wisps can be mistaken for detrusor (**muscularis propria**). Overcalling invasion as **pT2** instead of pT1 would push a patient toward cystectomy, so pathologists use smoothelin cautiously, and transurethral biopsies must include detrusor for adequate staging.

**Clinical correlates.** Defects of the glycosaminoglycan layer and barrier are proposed to underlie interstitial cystitis/bladder pain syndrome, which can cause **Hunner lesions**. Aristolochic acid causes upper-tract urothelial carcinoma. **Schistosoma haematobium** drives squamous carcinoma of the bladder.

**Recent advances.** Single-cell atlases of human urothelium are redefining its cell states. Organoids and tissue-engineered urothelium are being used to model infection and to work toward urethral reconstruction. Intravesical BCG for non-muscle-invasive cancer depends on how the urothelium interacts with the mycobacteria. Open questions include which progenitor cell gives rise to luminal versus basal tumor subtypes, and how stretch sensing by PIEZO channels shapes bladder overactivity.

keyPoints: Ureters, bladder and proximal urethra are lined by urothelium (transitional epithelium)
Urothelium has basal, intermediate and large umbrella cells
Uroplakin plaques (asymmetric unit membrane) make a near-waterproof barrier
Urothelium flattens when stretched; fusiform vesicles add apical membrane
Ureters move urine by peristalsis; oblique entry into the bladder limits reflux
The bladder's detrusor muscle empties it; the trigone has a smooth mucosa

test.q: Which epithelium lines the ureters and urinary bladder?
test.explain: Urothelium (transitional epithelium) lines the urinary passages from the calyces to the proximal urethra.

test.q: How does urothelium look when the bladder is full?
test.explain: Stretching flattens the cells, so the lining looks only 2-3 layers thick instead of 5-7.

test.q: The large, often binucleate surface cells of urothelium are called:
test.explain: Umbrella cells cap the urothelium and form its main barrier. Basal cells sit on the basement membrane instead.

test.q: What makes the umbrella cell's apical membrane rigid and impermeable?
test.explain: Uroplakin proteins form plaques of asymmetric unit membrane, which seal the surface against urine.

test.q: How does urine mainly travel down the ureter?
test.explain: Waves of smooth muscle contraction push urine along, which is why it still reaches the bladder when you lie down.

test.q: What prevents urine from flowing back up into the ureters?
choices: The ureters entering the bladder wall obliquely
A skeletal muscle sphincter at each orifice
test.explain: The oblique path through the wall acts as a flap valve that is compressed as the bladder fills.

test.q: The trigone of the bladder is notable because its mucosa:
choices: Is lined by simple squamous cells
Stays smooth when the bladder is empty
test.explain: The triangular trigone between the ureteric and urethral orifices has a smooth mucosa, unlike the folded rest of the empty bladder.

test.q: Classically, the muscle layers of the upper ureter are arranged as:
test.explain: The ureter is the reverse of the gut, with inner longitudinal and outer circular layers. The distal third adds an outer longitudinal layer.

test.q: As the bladder fills, how do umbrella cells add apical surface area?
choices: By dividing rapidly into many new cells
By fusing stored vesicles into it
By shedding their outer surface layer
By growing long motile surface cilia
test.explain: Fusiform vesicles carrying uroplakin plaques fuse with the apical membrane, and the extra membrane is retrieved after voiding.

test.q: What is the name of the bladder's main smooth muscle that contracts to empty it?
test.explain: The detrusor has three interwoven smooth muscle layers.

test.q: Urothelium is also called ___ epithelium because its appearance changes with stretch.
test.explain: Transitional epithelium is the older name for urothelium.

test.q: What tube carries urine from the bladder out of the body?
test.explain: The ureters bring urine to the bladder, and the urethra carries it out.

kidTest.q: What carries pee from the kidneys to the bladder?
kidTest.explain: Two thin tubes called ureters carry pee down to the bladder.

kidTest.q: What happens to the bladder lining cells when the bladder fills?
kidTest.explain: They stretch thin, like rolled-out dough.

kidTest.q: What job do the umbrella cells do?
choices: Squeeze pee down to the bladder
Keep pee out of body tissues
Give the pee its yellow color
kidTest.explain: Umbrella cells line the inside of the bladder. Like an umbrella, they form a tight barrier that keeps pee from seeping into the body's tissues. Muscle squeezes the pee along, and a pigment called urochrome makes it yellow.

kidTest.q: How do the ureters push pee along?
kidTest.explain: The muscles squeeze in waves, like squeezing toothpaste.

kidTest.q: What is the stretchy bag that holds pee? (b _ _ _ _ _ _)
kidTest.explain: The bladder stores pee until you go to the bathroom.

advancedTest.q: Mice lacking UPIIIa develop vesicoureteral reflux and a leaky urothelium. What does this best suggest?
choices: Uroplakin loss mainly increases detrusor pacemaking
Reflux is caused by uroplakin-driven crystal formation
Uroplakins aid both barrier and tract development
Uroplakins mainly serve as receptors for bacteria
advancedTest.explain: Losing UPIIIa disrupts plaques, causing a permeable barrier and urinary tract anomalies such as reflux and hydronephrosis. This shows uroplakins have both structural and developmental roles.

advancedTest.q: Why does a bladder infection often return even after the bacteria in the urine are cleared?
choices: Uroplakins rapidly digest antibiotics in urine
Type 1 pili make bacteria resist peristalsis
FimH blocks shedding of the umbrella cells
Bacteria persist quietly inside deeper cells
advancedTest.explain: After umbrella cells are shed, surviving bacteria can persist as quiescent reservoirs inside underlying cells and later re-emerge, causing a new infection.

advancedTest.q: A biopsy shows full-thickness CK20, loss of CD44 and an intact umbrella layer over atypical cells. What is the best interpretation?
choices: Reactive atypia, confirmed by the CK20 pattern
Carcinoma in situ remains likely despite the umbrella cells
Normal urothelium, since umbrella cells exclude malignancy
Nephrogenic adenoma, given its typical stain profile
advancedTest.explain: Umbrella cells can persist over CIS. Full-thickness CK20 with loss of CD44 supports carcinoma in situ rather than a reactive change.

advancedTest.q: Why is mistaking muscularis mucosae for muscularis propria in a bladder biopsy clinically serious?
choices: It upstages pT1 to pT2, which may prompt cystectomy
It hides any vascular invasion in the lamina propria
It changes the tumor grade but not its management
It causes a urothelial tumor to be called squamous
advancedTest.explain: Invasion into the detrusor (pT2) changes treatment dramatically, so misreading wisps of muscularis mucosae as detrusor overstages the tumor.

lessons.title: Pituitary & Pineal Glands

levels.kid:
Deep inside your head sit two tiny glands. A **gland** is a part of the body that makes messages called **hormones**.

The **pituitary** is about the size of a pea. It hangs under the brain like a cherry on a stem. People call it the "boss gland" because its messages tell other glands what to do. It helps you grow taller and helps your body handle stress.

The pituitary has two parts. The front part is a factory that makes hormones. The back part is more like a mailbox. The brain sends hormones down the stem, and the back part sends them out into the blood.

The **pineal** gland is shaped like a tiny pine cone. When it gets dark, it makes **melatonin**, a message that helps you feel sleepy.
levels.hs:
The **pituitary gland** (hypophysis) sits in a bony pocket of the skull called the **sella turcica**, connected to the brain's **hypothalamus** by a stalk. Under the microscope it is really two different organs joined together:

- **Anterior pituitary (adenohypophysis)**: true glandular tissue. It forms in the embryo from an upgrowth of the roof of the mouth called **Rathke's pouch**. Its cells sit in cords next to wide, leaky capillaries.
- **Posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis)**: an extension of the brain. It is mostly nerve fibers whose cell bodies live in the hypothalamus.

With standard stains, anterior cells come in three looks. **Acidophils** stain pink and make growth hormone and prolactin. **Basophils** stain blue-purple and make TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH. **Chromophobes** stain pale.

The posterior lobe releases **oxytocin** and **antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**, also called vasopressin. Both are made in the hypothalamus and carried down the axons. Bulges of stored hormone along those axons are called **Herring bodies**.

The **pineal gland** sits at the back of the third ventricle. Its main cells, **pinealocytes**, make **melatonin** at night. A real example: with age, the pineal collects calcium deposits called **brain sand** (corpora arenacea). These show up on X-rays and CT scans, and radiologists have long used them as a midline landmark.
levels.college:
**Pituitary architecture.** The hypophysis has two embryologic origins, and each gives it a different tissue type.

- **Adenohypophysis**, from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch). It has three parts: the **pars distalis** (the bulk), the **pars tuberalis** (wrapping the stalk), and the **pars intermedia** (rudimentary in humans, often marked by colloid-filled **Rathke's cysts**).
- **Neurohypophysis**, from neuroectoderm (the diencephalic floor). It has three parts: the **median eminence**, the **infundibulum**, and the **pars nervosa**.

**The hypophyseal portal system.** Superior hypophyseal arteries form a primary capillary plexus in the median eminence. There, hypothalamic neurons release releasing and inhibiting hormones such as TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH, somatostatin and dopamine. **Portal veins** run down the stalk to a secondary plexus of **fenestrated sinusoidal capillaries** in the pars distalis. This means the hypothalamus controls the anterior lobe with hormones carried in blood, not with nerves.

**Pars distalis cell types** (immunohistochemistry is the modern standard):
- Acidophils: **somatotrophs** (GH), the most numerous at about 50%, and **lactotrophs** (PRL).
- Basophils: **corticotrophs** (ACTH, from POMC), **thyrotrophs** (TSH) and **gonadotrophs** (FSH/LH). Thyrotrophs and gonadotrophs secrete glycoproteins, so they are PAS-positive.
- Chromophobes: degranulated or nonsecretory cells, plus **folliculostellate cells**.

**Pars nervosa.** Unmyelinated axons come from the **supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei**. Their terminals end on fenestrated capillaries. Supporting glia called **pituicytes** surround them, along with Herring bodies.

**Pineal gland.** It is covered by pia and divided into lobules. It contains:
- **Pinealocytes**, modified neurons with long processes.
- Interstitial astrocyte-like glia.
- Corpora arenacea, made of calcium phosphate and carbonate.

Its sympathetic input arrives from the **superior cervical ganglion**. This input relays light information from the retina through the suprachiasmatic nucleus. The pineal secretes melatonin when it is dark.
levels.phd:
**Development and lineage.** Rathke's pouch invaginates from stomodeal ectoderm by about week 4. It is induced by the overlying infundibulum through FGF8, BMP4 and SHH signaling. Anterior pituitary lineages are specified by transcription factors:
- **PIT1 (POU1F1)** for somatotrophs, lactotrophs and thyrotrophs.
- **TPIT (TBX19)** for corticotrophs.
- **SF1 (NR5A1)** for gonadotrophs.

PROP1 acts upstream of PIT1. Its mutations are the most common genetic cause of combined pituitary hormone deficiency. These lineage factors now anchor tumor classification, as discussed below.

**Mosaic organization.** The pars distalis is not a random scatter of cells. Imaging studies by Mollard, Bonnefont and colleagues showed that somatotrophs and other lineages form **three-dimensional homotypic networks** linked by gap junctions and adherens junctions. These networks coordinate pulsatile secretion and remodel with physiological demand, for example lactotroph network plasticity in lactation. Folliculostellate cells, which are S100-positive, form a separate gap-junction-coupled syncytium. They may relay paracrine signals.

**Stem cells.** **SOX2-positive cells** in the marginal zone lining Rathke's cleft act as adult progenitors. Lineage tracing shows they contribute to cell turnover. SOX2-positive cells can also drive tumorigenesis paracrinally when they express oncogenic β-catenin. This links them to adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma, which carries *CTNNB1* mutations.

**Posterior lobe.** Magnocellular neurons package oxytocin or vasopressin with their carrier proteins, the **neurophysins**. The packaging begins in the Golgi and the hormones travel by fast axonal transport. Pituicytes express TTF1 and can retract to change how much axon terminal contacts the perivascular space.

**Pineal.** Norepinephrine acts on β1-adrenergic receptors and raises cAMP. This upregulates **arylalkylamine N-acetyltransferase (AANAT)**, the rate-limiting enzyme, which converts serotonin to N-acetylserotonin. **ASMT (HIOMT)** then produces melatonin. Light at night rapidly suppresses AANAT activity through proteasomal degradation. Retinal input reaches the SCN via intrinsically photosensitive ganglion cells expressing **melanopsin**. Pineal calcification is a subject of debate. It correlates with age, but whether it reduces melatonin output is still argued.
levels.expert:
**Neurosurgical relevance.** Pituitary neuroendocrine tumors are among the most common intracranial neoplasms. Since the 2017 and 2022 WHO classifications, the term **PitNET** has partly replaced "adenoma." They are typed by lineage transcription factor (PIT1, TPIT, SF1, or none) plus hormone immunohistochemistry, not by H&E staining.

High-risk subtypes include:
- **Sparsely granulated somatotroph** tumors. These show fibrous bodies, seen as paranuclear keratin dots with CAM5.2.
- **Silent corticotroph** tumors.
- **Crooke cell** tumors.
- **Immature PIT1-lineage** tumors.
- **Null-cell** tumors.

The term "pituitary carcinoma" was replaced in 2022 by "metastatic PitNET."

**Pathologist pitfalls.**
- **Crooke's hyaline change.** Hyaline keratin builds up in non-tumorous corticotrophs when glucocorticoid levels are high. It is a marker of hypercortisolism from any cause, not a tumor.
- **Normal gland in a sample.** It can be hard to tell normal gland in a transsphenoidal specimen from a tumor. Reticulin stain helps. The normal acinar reticulin network is disrupted in PitNETs.
- **Physiologic enlargement.** Lactotroph hyperplasia in pregnancy enlarges the gland and can mimic a tumor on MRI.

**Differential of sellar masses.**
- **Adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma**: wet keratin, stellate reticulum, calcification.
- **Papillary craniopharyngioma**: *BRAF V600E*, which is targetable with BRAF/MEK inhibitors.
- **Rathke cleft cyst**: ciliated or mucinous epithelium.
- **Pituicytoma** and **spindle cell oncocytoma**: both are TTF1-positive and now viewed as one posterior-lobe tumor family.
- **Lymphocytic hypophysitis**, including immune-checkpoint-inhibitor hypophysitis, which notably targets corticotrophs.

**Imaging-histology correlation.** On T1 MRI the posterior lobe shows a **bright spot**. This is attributed to vasopressin-neurophysin granules, and it may disappear in central diabetes insipidus.

**Pineal region.** The **pineocytoma–pineoblastoma** spectrum covers pineal parenchymal tumors. Between them sits the intermediate-differentiation tumor, PPTID, which carries *KBTBD4* insertions. Other pineal-region tumors include:
- Germinomas, which are PLAP/OCT4-positive and stand out for their two-cell pattern with lymphocytes.
- Papillary tumor of the pineal region.

Pineal cysts are common incidental findings. Parinaud syndrome signals tectal compression.

**Open questions.**
- How plastic are the homotypic cell networks in human disease?
- Can SOX2-positive progenitors be harnessed for regeneration?
- Does pineal calcification have real functional significance for circadian disorders?
- How should transcription-factor classification shape adjuvant therapy?

keyPoints: Anterior pituitary is glandular (Rathke's pouch); posterior pituitary is neural tissue
Hypophyseal portal veins carry hypothalamic hormones to the anterior lobe
Acidophils make GH and prolactin; basophils make TSH, ACTH, FSH and LH
Posterior lobe stores oxytocin and ADH in Herring bodies, supported by pituicytes
Pinealocytes make melatonin at night via sympathetic input and AANAT
Brain sand (corpora arenacea) calcifies the pineal with age

test.q: The anterior pituitary develops from which embryonic structure?
test.explain: The adenohypophysis comes from oral ectoderm (Rathke's pouch). The posterior lobe comes from the diencephalic floor.

test.q: Which cells of the pars distalis secrete growth hormone?
test.explain: Somatotrophs are acidophils that make GH. They are the most numerous anterior pituitary cell type.

test.q: How do hypothalamic releasing hormones reach the anterior lobe?
test.explain: The portal system carries releasing hormones from the median eminence to the sinusoids of the pars distalis. Axonal transport serves the posterior lobe instead.

test.q: Herring bodies are best described as:
choices: Glial cells of the posterior lobe
Colloid cysts of the intermediate lobe
test.explain: Herring bodies are swellings of hypothalamic axons filled with oxytocin or ADH granules. Pituicytes are the glia.

test.q: Which hormone is made by a basophil?
test.explain: Corticotrophs (basophils) make ACTH. Prolactin and GH come from acidophils, and oxytocin is released from the posterior lobe.

test.q: Where are the cell bodies of the neurons that end in the pars nervosa?
test.explain: Magnocellular neurons in the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei send axons to the posterior lobe.

test.q: The main secretory cell of the pineal gland is the:
test.explain: Pinealocytes, modified neurons, make melatonin. Pituicytes belong to the posterior pituitary.

test.q: What type of capillaries supplies the pars distalis?
test.explain: Wide fenestrated sinusoids let hormones pass easily between the blood and the gland cells.

test.q: Pineal melatonin secretion rises mainly in response to:
test.explain: Darkness boosts sympathetic input to the pineal, which raises melatonin. Light suppresses it.

test.q: What is the bony skull pocket that holds the pituitary called?
test.explain: The sella turcica of the sphenoid bone houses the hypophysis.

test.q: Calcified pineal deposits are commonly called brain ___.
test.explain: Brain sand (corpora arenacea) increases with age and is visible on imaging.

test.q: What glial cells support the axons of the posterior pituitary?
test.explain: Pituicytes are the specialized glia of the neurohypophysis.

kidTest.q: About how big is the pituitary gland?
kidTest.explain: The pituitary is about pea-sized.

kidTest.q: Why is the pituitary called the boss gland?
choices: It pumps blood through your body
It tells other glands what to do
It is the biggest gland in your body
kidTest.explain: Its hormones give orders to other glands.

kidTest.q: What is the pineal gland shaped like?
kidTest.explain: Pineal comes from the Latin word for pine cone, which the gland's shape resembles.

kidTest.q: What does the back part of the pituitary act like?
kidTest.explain: It stores brain hormones and sends them out, like a mailbox.

kidTest.q: Which sleepy hormone does the pineal make at night? m _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Melatonin helps you feel sleepy when it is dark.

advancedTest.q: A transsphenoidal specimen shows intact acinar reticulin with mixed cell types. The most reasonable reading is:
advancedTest.explain: PitNETs disrupt the reticulin network. An intact acinar pattern with a mixed population suggests normal gland.

advancedTest.q: Crooke's hyaline change in corticotrophs is best read as evidence of:
choices: A corticotroph tumor in that region
advancedTest.explain: Keratin accumulates in non-tumorous corticotrophs under high cortisol, whatever the source. It does not localize a tumor.

advancedTest.q: A loss of the posterior pituitary T1 bright spot fits best with:
advancedTest.explain: The bright spot reflects stored vasopressin-neurophysin granules, which are depleted in central diabetes insipidus.

advancedTest.q: Light at night lowers melatonin quickly mainly because:
choices: Serotonin synthesis in pinealocytes is blocked
Pinealocytes rapidly lose their β1 receptors
advancedTest.explain: Loss of adrenergic drive lets the rate-limiting AANAT be rapidly degraded by proteasomes, which cuts melatonin output.

lessons.title: Thyroid, Parathyroid & Adrenal Glands

levels.kid:
Your body has tiny factories that make messages called **hormones**. Three of them sit in your neck and on top of your kidneys.

The **thyroid** is shaped like a butterfly in your neck. Under a microscope it looks like lots of little round balloons. Each balloon is filled with pink jelly, which stores hormone until the body needs it.

Behind the thyroid are four tiny **parathyroid** glands, each about the size of a grain of rice. They keep calcium in your blood just right, so your bones and muscles work.

On top of each kidney sits an **adrenal** gland, like a little hat. Its outside layer makes stress and salt hormones. Its middle makes adrenaline, the "run fast!" hormone.
levels.hs:
**Endocrine glands** release hormones straight into the blood instead of through ducts, so they are packed with capillaries.

**Thyroid.** Its basic unit is the **follicle**: a hollow sphere lined by one layer of **follicular cells** (cuboidal epithelium) around a pink gel called **colloid**. Colloid is made mostly of **thyroglobulin**, a protein that stores thyroid hormones (T3 and T4). These hormones set the body's metabolic rate and need iodine. Between follicles are pale **parafollicular (C) cells**, which make **calcitonin**.

**Parathyroid.** There are usually four small glands on the back of the thyroid. Most cells are **chief cells**, which secrete **parathyroid hormone (PTH)**. PTH raises blood calcium by acting on bone, kidney and, indirectly, the gut. Larger pink **oxyphil cells** become more common with age, and fat cells also increase over the years.

**Adrenal gland.** It has two parts with different origins:
- The **cortex**, with three layers that make steroid hormones: aldosterone (salt balance), cortisol (stress and blood sugar) and androgens.
- The **medulla**, which makes epinephrine (adrenaline) and norepinephrine.

Real example: in **Graves' disease**, antibodies overstimulate the thyroid. The follicular cells grow tall, and the colloid looks scalloped because it is being used up fast.
levels.college:
**Thyroid histology.** A fibrous capsule sends septa into the gland, dividing it into lobules of follicles. The height of the follicular epithelium reflects activity:
- **Squamous to low cuboidal** cells with abundant colloid mean an inactive gland.
- **Tall columnar** cells with scant, peripherally scalloped colloid (resorption vacuoles) mean an active gland.

Hormone synthesis runs in two directions. Cells secrete thyroglobulin apically into the follicle lumen. They take up iodide basolaterally via the **Na⁺/I⁻ symporter (NIS)** and pass it to the lumen via **pendrin**. At the apical membrane, **thyroid peroxidase (TPO)** oxidizes iodide and attaches it to tyrosine residues on thyroglobulin, forming MIT and DIT, then couples them into T3 and T4. When **TSH** stimulates the cell, it engulfs colloid by endocytosis, lysosomes cleave the hormone free, and T4 and T3 leave basally into fenestrated capillaries. **C cells** come from the neural crest via the ultimobranchial body and sit within the follicle basal lamina or between follicles.

**Parathyroid.** Cords of **chief cells** lie amid capillaries. Chief cells sense calcium through the **calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR)**. **Oxyphil cells** are packed with mitochondria, so they stain intensely eosinophilic. Adipocytes accumulate with age.

**Adrenal cortex** (mesodermal origin), from capsule inward ("GFR" makes "salt, sugar, sex"):
- **Zona glomerulosa**: arched clusters of cells that make **aldosterone**, controlled by angiotensin II and K⁺.
- **Zona fasciculata**: the thickest layer, made of radial cords of lipid-laden "spongiocytes" that make **cortisol** under ACTH control.
- **Zona reticularis**: an anastomosing network of cells with **lipofuscin** that makes DHEA and other androgens.

Steroid-producing cells have abundant smooth ER, lipid droplets and mitochondria with tubular cristae.

**Adrenal medulla** (neural crest origin). **Chromaffin cells** are modified postganglionic sympathetic neurons innervated by preganglionic fibers. The **chromaffin reaction** browns them because catecholamines oxidize with chromium salts.
levels.phd:
**Blood supply and zonation.** The adrenal cortex drains centripetally through sinusoids. Cortisol-rich blood therefore bathes the medulla and induces **PNMT**, the enzyme that methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine. This portal-like arrangement explains why about 80% of medullary output is epinephrine. Medullary arteries also deliver blood directly.

Zonation is enzymatic:
- The glomerulosa expresses **CYP11B2** (aldosterone synthase) and lacks CYP17A1.
- The fasciculata expresses **CYP11B1** and CYP17A1 hydroxylase activity.
- The reticularis expresses cytochrome b5, which favors the 17,20-lyase reaction and therefore androgen output.

Cortical renewal shows **centripetal migration**. Lineage tracing (e.g., Freedman et al., 2013) indicates that capsular and subcapsular progenitors marked by Shh and Gli1 give rise to glomerulosa cells. These cells then convert to fasciculata cells as they move inward, a process regulated by Wnt/β-catenin (glomerulosa) and PKA/ACTH (fasciculata) signaling. The fetal adrenal has a large **fetal zone** that makes DHEA-S, a substrate for placental estrogen; this zone involutes after birth.

**Thyroid biochemistry.** TPO needs H₂O₂ produced by **DUOX2** with its maturation factor DUOXA2. Iodotyrosine deiodinase (**DEHAL1**) recycles iodide from MIT and DIT. The **Wolff–Chaikoff effect** (1948) is an acute shutdown of organification caused by excess iodide; the gland normally escapes it by downregulating NIS. Iodinated thyroglobulin, about 660 kDa, is reabsorbed by macropinocytosis and by megalin-mediated endocytosis. Thyroglobulin is digested by cathepsins, and **MCT8** exports the hormone. Most circulating T3 comes from peripheral **D1/D2 deiodination** of T4.

**Parathyroid.** CaSR is a class C GPCR. Its activation lowers PTH secretion and, more slowly, reduces gland proliferation. FGF23 and 1,25(OH)₂D also suppress PTH. Inactivating CaSR mutations cause **familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia**. The physiological role of oxyphil cells remains debated. They may be transformed chief cells: they show CaSR and PTH expression, and they expand in secondary hyperparathyroidism of chronic kidney disease.

**Development.** The thyroid forms from an endodermal diverticulum at the foramen cecum (transcription factors NKX2-1, PAX8 and FOXE1). The inferior parathyroids come from the 3rd pharyngeal pouch, together with the thymus, and the superior parathyroids from the 4th pouch.
levels.expert:
**Diagnostic histology pitfalls.**
- **Papillary thyroid carcinoma** is diagnosed by nuclear features, not architecture: enlarged, overlapping, clear ("Orphan Annie") nuclei with grooves and pseudoinclusions; psammoma bodies support the diagnosis. **NIFTP** was reclassified in 2016 as a noninvasive, low-risk neoplasm to curb overtreatment.
- **Follicular adenoma versus carcinoma** cannot be separated on fine-needle aspiration cytology. The distinction needs capsular or vascular invasion on the resected specimen, which is why Bethesda category IV nodules go to lobectomy or molecular testing (e.g., Afirma, ThyroSeq).
- **Medullary carcinoma** arises from C cells. It shows amyloid made of calcitonin, stains for calcitonin and CEA, and is linked to **RET** mutations in MEN2. C-cell hyperplasia is its precursor in familial cases.
- In **Hashimoto thyroiditis**, lymphoid follicles with germinal centers and Hürthle (oncocytic) cells are typical. There is an increased risk of thyroid MALT lymphoma.

**Parathyroid.** Intraoperatively, an adenoma usually shows chief cells with little or no stromal fat and a compressed rim of normal gland, but histology alone poorly separates adenoma from hyperplasia. Surgeons therefore rely on **intraoperative PTH** monitoring: a fall of more than 50% about 10 minutes after excision (the Miami criterion). Localization uses sestamibi scanning, 4D-CT or **18F-fluorocholine PET**. Loss of **parafibromin** (CDC73) immunostaining flags carcinoma or hyperparathyroidism–jaw tumor syndrome.

**Adrenal.** Pharmacology maps neatly onto the zones:
- **Metyrapone** blocks CYP11B1, and osilodrostat blocks both CYP11B1 and CYP11B2.
- **Mitotane** is adrenolytic, causing necrosis of the fasciculata and reticularis.
- Exogenous glucocorticoids suppress ACTH and atrophy the fasciculata while sparing the glomerulosa. This is why secondary adrenal insufficiency rarely causes salt-wasting crisis.

**Aldosterone-producing micronodules** (formerly cell clusters), revealed by CYP11B2 immunohistochemistry and carrying KCNJ5 or CACNA1D mutations, are reshaping models of primary aldosteronism. Adrenocortical carcinoma is diagnosed (benign versus malignant) with the **Weiss score**.

**Pheochromocytoma** shows a "Zellballen" nest pattern with S100-positive sustentacular cells. **SDHB** immunostaining loss flags germline SDHx mutations. Every pheochromocytoma is considered metastasis-capable.

For neurosurgeons, **Cushing disease** (pituitary ACTH excess) produces bilateral fasciculata hyperplasia. A **Crooke hyaline change** in the non-tumoral corticotrophs confirms glucocorticoid excess. Open questions include zonal plasticity in humans and the human relevance of adrenal capsule stem cells.

keyPoints: Thyroid follicles: follicular cells around colloid made of thyroglobulin
Taller follicular cells and scalloped colloid indicate an active thyroid
Parafollicular C cells (neural crest) secrete calcitonin
Parathyroid chief cells secrete PTH; oxyphil cells increase with age
Adrenal cortex zones G-F-R make aldosterone, cortisol, androgens (salt, sugar, sex)
Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells make catecholamines; cortisol induces PNMT

test.q: The pink gel inside a thyroid follicle is called:
test.explain: Colloid fills the follicle lumen and is mostly thyroglobulin, which stores thyroid hormone.

test.q: Which cells secrete calcitonin?
test.explain: Parafollicular (C) cells, derived from the neural crest, make calcitonin. Chief cells make PTH, not calcitonin.

test.q: A highly active thyroid follicle typically shows:
test.explain: Active follicles have tall columnar cells, and their colloid is scalloped at the edge where it is being resorbed.

test.q: Parathyroid hormone is made mainly by:
test.explain: Chief cells secrete PTH and sense calcium through the calcium-sensing receptor.

test.q: Which adrenal cortical zone produces aldosterone?
test.explain: The outermost zone, the glomerulosa, makes aldosterone. The fasciculata makes cortisol.

test.q: The thickest layer of the adrenal cortex, with lipid-laden spongiocytes, is the:
test.explain: The fasciculata is the thickest zone; its cells are packed with lipid and make cortisol under ACTH control.

test.q: Adrenal medulla chromaffin cells are best described as modified:
test.explain: Chromaffin cells come from the neural crest and act as postganglionic sympathetic neurons, receiving preganglionic input.

test.q: Which enzyme iodinates tyrosines on thyroglobulin?
test.explain: TPO oxidizes iodide and attaches it to thyroglobulin at the apical membrane. NIS and pendrin are transporters.

test.q: Organelles typical of steroid-making adrenal cortical cells include:
choices: Abundant rough ER and secretory granules
test.explain: Steroidogenic cells have abundant smooth ER, lipid droplets and mitochondria with tubular cristae.

test.q: Colloid is made mostly of the protein ___.
test.explain: Thyroglobulin is the scaffold on which T3 and T4 are built and stored.

test.q: What hormone does the zona fasciculata mainly produce?
test.explain: The fasciculata makes the glucocorticoid cortisol under ACTH control.

test.q: Pink, mitochondria-rich parathyroid cells that increase with age are called ___ cells.
test.explain: Oxyphil cells are eosinophilic because they are packed with mitochondria.

kidTest.q: Where is the thyroid gland?
kidTest.explain: The butterfly-shaped thyroid sits in the front of your neck.

kidTest.q: What do parathyroid glands help control?
kidTest.explain: They keep blood calcium at the right level for bones and muscles.

kidTest.q: Where do the adrenal glands sit?
kidTest.explain: They sit on top of the kidneys like little hats.

kidTest.q: The middle of the adrenal gland makes which hormone?
kidTest.explain: Adrenaline is the "run fast!" hormone made in the adrenal middle.

kidTest.q: Chemical messages made by glands are called h _ _ _ _ _ _ s.
kidTest.explain: Hormones travel in the blood to give the body messages.

advancedTest.q: Why is most adrenal medullary output epinephrine rather than norepinephrine?
choices: Chromaffin cells lack dopamine beta-hydroxylase activity
Cortisol in centripetal blood induces PNMT
advancedTest.explain: Cortisol-rich blood flowing inward from the cortex induces PNMT, which methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine.

advancedTest.q: A patient on long-term exogenous glucocorticoids is least likely to show which change?
advancedTest.explain: The glomerulosa is driven mainly by angiotensin II and K⁺, not ACTH, so aldosterone is preserved even as the fasciculata atrophies.

advancedTest.q: Why can't fine-needle cytology separate follicular adenoma from carcinoma?
choices: Carcinoma needs capsular or vascular invasion on resection
Both lack thyroglobulin in their cells
Adenomas show nuclear grooves and pseudoinclusions
Carcinoma is defined by amyloid deposits
advancedTest.explain: Malignancy in follicular neoplasms is defined by invasion, which only a resected specimen can show. Nuclear features define papillary carcinoma instead.

advancedTest.q: An inactivating CaSR mutation would be expected to produce:
choices: Low PTH with low blood calcium
advancedTest.explain: Chief cells sense calcium poorly, so they keep secreting PTH at higher calcium levels, as in familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.
